blocks.text: 37.1 grams of fat. The bright spot is 5.8 grams of polyunsaturated fat, which helps balance the fat profile. The pressure point is 12.6 grams of saturated fat. For meats, fat quality matters because the protein can be good, but the fat decides how clean the tradeoff feels.
Carbs are basically out of the picture here. There are no defensible carb submacros to score, so this section does not really help or hurt bacon in the way it would for grains, fruits, or tubers.

13.7 grams of protein. Essential amino acids land at 9 out of 9, so the protein has a real repair and maintenance role. Non-essential amino acids are also strong at 10 out of 11, while collagen is only 0.4 grams. For meats, protein quality is the main reason this entry stays interesting.

Vitamin B12 is the clear vitamin mark at 21% daily value, supporting nerves and blood cells. Vitamin D is only 1% daily value, and the rest of the vitamin panel is thin, so bacon is not carrying the broad micronutrient workload you might want from a meat.
Zinc is the best mineral mark at 10% daily value, with a modest immune-support angle. Iron is only 2% daily value and potassium is 4%, so the mineral section is mostly weak for a meat entry.

Pros first: highly palatable and appealing. It is an obvious reason people like it. Works as a strong flavour booster. A small amount can carry a whole plate. Has strong comfort-food appeal. It is instantly recognisable and easy to package in meals.

The drawbacks next: sodium is a major drawback. Processing is a major negative. Salty-fatty profile encourages portion creep. Those three cons matter because bacon is built to be easy to keep eating, not easy to moderate.

So Bacon has real protein quality, useful vitamin B12, and a strong flavour role. But saturated fat, low vitamin D, low iron, heavy sodium, processing, and portion creep pull it down hard. It is best as a small flavour tool or occasional comfort-food add-on, not as a core everyday protein.
